title: Scones
subtitle: Light and tall British cream tea scones with sultanas
excerpt: High-rising, fluffy scones with a crisp top and soft crumb, packed with plump sultanas and ready in under 30 minutes. Split and served with clotted cream and jam.

recipe.sourceNotes: Scones are a central fixture of British afternoon tea and are particularly associated with the cream teas of Devon and Cornwall, where a long-running dispute about whether cream or jam should go on first continues. The Devon tradition puts cream on first, then jam; the Cornish tradition reverses the order. The scone itself is a quick bread leavened with baking powder, and its origins lie in Scotland, where the word scone (possibly from the Scots Gaelic sgonn) originally referred to a flat, unleavened griddle bread. The modern oven-baked scone with baking powder dates from the nineteenth century. The keys to a well-risen scone are: very cold butter rubbed in lightly, a light hand when mixing, the dough handled as little as possible, and the cutter pressed straight down without twisting. Twisting the cutter seals the edges and prevents the scone from rising straight. Scones should be eaten on the day of baking.

recipeTools.notes: A baking tray lined with baking parchment. A 6 cm round plain cutter.

content.text: Use cold butter straight from the fridge: the small pockets of cold fat in the dough create steam as they melt in the oven, which pushes the scones up. Warm butter blends into the flour and makes a flat, greasy scone. Work fast and handle the dough as little as possible: overworked dough makes tough scones. When cutting out, press the cutter straight down and lift straight up without any twisting motion. Brush the tops with egg wash but do not let it run down the sides, as this will prevent the scones from rising evenly.

Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Put the flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl. Add the cold butter cubes and rub in with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar and sultanas.

Make a well in the centre. Pour in most of the milk and mix quickly with a round-bladed knife until the dough just comes together. Add a little more milk if necessary to bring it to a soft but not sticky dough. Do not over-mix.

Turn out onto a lightly floured surface and pat to 3 cm thick. Cut out rounds with a 6 cm cutter, pressing straight down without twisting. Place on the lined baking tray. Brush the tops with beaten egg. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until risen and golden. Cool briefly on a wire rack. Serve warm.
